title: Final review week
intro: Use this plan in the last 7 days before CIA Part 3, after you have worked through the notes and taken your mocks. Nothing in it is new. Most days take about an hour; the two mock days and the day after the full mock take longer.
how_it_works: No new topics this week. Late new material crowds out what you have already learned.
One full timed mock at the start of the week, then no more full mocks. The last days are for recall and rest.
Answer from memory first, then check. Recalling builds memory; rereading mostly makes pages feel familiar.
Time follows the exam weights, so Section D, the largest at 45%, gets the most, then Section A at 25%. Sections B and C, 15% each, share a day.
Part 3 turns on close pairs: approve or tell, must or should, function or engagement. A few minutes a day on these pairs keeps them apart.
Memory settles while you sleep, so a full night's rest is part of the plan. Missed a day? Skip it and carry on; never double up.

days.title: Full rehearsal
days.goal: Sit one full timed mock at the real length, ideally at your exam's start time, to rehearse pace and stamina.

tasks.text: Warm up for five minutes: say how a finding fixed before issue appears in the final communication, and what follows a significant error found after issue. Then check the note.
Say your seat in one line: the chief audit executive proposes, reports and escalates; the board approves; management owns the fix. Then check the principle.
Take a full timed mock in one sitting: 100 questions in 120 minutes, phone away, no notes.
Pace by two checkpoints: question 50 by minute 60; question 75 by minute 90. Stuck on one? Choose your best answer, flag it and move on.
Your misses go to your mistake journal on their own. Rest tonight and review them tomorrow.

days.remember: A mock is a rehearsal, not a verdict. KaiSip shows percent by section; that is not The IIA's scaled score and cannot predict your result.

days.title: Learn from your misses
days.goal: Trace each mock miss to its thinking slip, then recall Section D, the largest at 45%. Stop at about 90 minutes.

tasks.text: In your mistake journal, review each miss from the mock, newest first.
Tag why you missed each one: “Acted as the wrong person”, “Missed ‘first’ or ‘best’”, “Tool before policy”, “Fixed the symptom, not the cause”, “Misread” or “Didn’t know it”.
Read the principles behind the slip you tagged most often.
From memory, list five Section D points, from the final communication to escalation. Then open the list and check.
Say the steps for risk accepted above appetite or tolerance, in order, with must or should for each. Then check the note.

days.remember: Accepted risk climbs in order: the responsible management, senior management, then the board if unresolved. The chief audit executive raises it and never resolves it.

days.title: The three close pairs
days.goal: Drill the pairs Part 3 turns on, recall Section A, and work on the section furthest behind its weight.

tasks.text: Approve or tell: which plan matters does the board approve, which are only reported in time, and what happens with an urgent change? Check the note.
Must or should: sort the conformance statement, the board's private meeting and the three steps for accepted risk. Then check the principles on reading the question.
Function or engagement: name two decisions that are the chief audit executive's for the whole function, and two that belong to one engagement. Then read the principles on your seat.
From memory, list five Section A points: providers, budget, people, strategy and reporting. Then open the list and check.
Answer a short untimed set in your focus section. Before each answer, name the actor and whether the question asks for a must or a should.

days.remember: The board approves the charter, plan, significant changes and budget. Asked what is required, a should loses; asked what comes first, it can win.

days.title: Pace check
days.goal: Keep your pace sharp with one short timed mock, then recall the final communication, follow-up and escalation, and the function's independence.

tasks.text: Take the short timed mock in one sitting. Watch your pace more than the score.
From memory, list what every final communication holds and what an assurance one adds. Then check the note.
Say how follow-up works and who acts when a date is missed, in order. Then read the principles on speaking up.
Before you open it, say why repairing the items found is not a fix, and why assurance is never a guarantee. Then check the principles on proving it.
Say how often the chief audit executive confirms the function's independence to the board, and who hears about a threat to it. Then check the principles on staying unbiased.

days.remember: This is your last timed test before the exam. From here, short recall keeps you sharp.

days.title: The plan and quality
days.goal: Recall Sections B and C from the chief audit executive's seat, sharpen how you read questions, and work on your second gap.

tasks.text: From memory, list three Section B points and three Section C points, and say who approves in each. Then open the lists and check.
Say how a nonconformance is disclosed for one engagement and for the whole function. Then check the note.
Say what must set the plan and what you tell the board when it cannot cover a high-risk area. Then check the principles on what drives the work.
Redo your mistake journal questions. Before you choose, say why your old answer loses.
Practice a short untimed set in your second-weakest section. Find the priority word before you read the options.

days.remember: A request is an input, not an order, and reliance follows evaluation. Quality is shown with results; a nonconformance is disclosed, never hidden.

days.title: Light review and logistics
days.goal: Touch everything once, lightly, and settle the practical details so nothing on the day is a surprise.

tasks.text: For each section, recall two points before you open its list, starting with Section D. If one will not come back, open its note for that point only.
Say the seven priority words and the answering steps from memory, then check them.
Say the three pairs once more: approve or tell, must or should, function or engagement. Then glance at the one-line rules.
Look up any term on the lists that still feels fuzzy.
Confirm your appointment, the test center's address and your route. Read the ID and check-in rules in The IIA's candidate handbook.

days.remember: Recall beats rereading. Leave new material alone now.

days.title: The eve
days.goal: Stay fresh, not tired: a light touch in the morning, then rest.

tasks.text: Optional: say the answering steps and your two checkpoints from memory, then check them. Stop after 15 minutes.
Read the one-line rule for your most common slip on the principles list.
Work through the eve checklist.
Close the books by early evening and keep your usual bedtime.

days.remember: Rest is part of the plan. If sleep comes slowly tonight, that is common, and your preparation is already done.

eve: Your appointment is confirmed, and you have read the ID and check-in rules in The IIA's current candidate handbook.
Your route to the test center and your travel time are planned, with a backup.
Your ID is laid out where you will see it in the morning.
You have read the reminder for your most common slip.
Skip alcohol tonight; it makes sleep lighter.
If worries keep circling, write them down for a few minutes, then put the page away.
Books are closed by early evening, and you keep your usual bedtime.
morning: Eat a familiar breakfast and keep your usual caffeine.
Reread your two checkpoints: question 50 by minute 60; question 75 by minute 90.
Leave early enough that a delay on the way would not matter.
Your seat: the chief audit executive running the function. You propose, report and escalate; the board approves, senior management supports, and management owns the fix.
A racing heart is your body getting ready. Treat it as energy for focus, not a sign of danger.
If your mind goes blank, breathe out slowly, pick your best answer for now and move on.

points.text: Outsource the work, never the responsibility. Contracted auditors follow the Standards, the chief audit executive supervises their engagements as for staff, and the board still approves an adequate budget.

Set the mix of assurance and advisory work through the function's methodology. Conflicting demands and high-risk areas left without assurance go to the board and senior management; the board approves significant plan changes.
Methodologies stay current: the chief audit executive evaluates and updates them after significant change in standards, law, technology or the team, and trains the auditors on them.
Build the budget from the strategy and plan, and seek the board's approval. When money falls short, promptly report the impact to the board and senior management; never trim the plan quietly.

The strategy holds a vision, strategic objectives and initiatives for the next few years, reviewed periodically with the board and senior management. No Standard asks the board to approve it; the plan is approved.
Report formally, relate informally. Give the board what it needs for oversight, not only what it asks for. Meeting the board privately at least once a year is a should.

Confirm the function's organizational independence to the board at least yearly, with any impairment and its safeguards, and raise potential impairments with the board and senior management. Risk accepted above appetite or tolerance is separate: it takes Standard 11.5's route.

The plan rests on a written, at least yearly risk assessment that covers the organization's strategy, objectives and risks, informed by the board and senior management. An audit universe is a tool, not a rule.
A request is an input, not an order. Weigh it against risk and resources, and report conflicting demands between major stakeholders to the board and senior management.
A Topical Requirement applies when its topic is planned, arises in an engagement or is requested. An audit cycle says when to look again, never how big the risk is.
Tell the board and senior management in time what the plan cannot cover and why: resource limits, a high-risk area left without assurance, scope or access limits. Telling is the must here.

The chief audit executive discusses the plan and significant changes with the board and senior management; the board approves both. An urgent change: inform the board at once, approve formally soon after.
Coordinate with other assurance providers to close gaps and cut duplication. When coordination fails, raise it with senior management first and the board if necessary.
Rely on another provider's work only after evaluating it, and document the basis. The chief audit executive stays responsible for internal audit's conclusions.

domains.name: Quality of the Internal Audit Function

points.text: The quality program covers the whole function through internal and external assessments. The chief audit executive owns it and may delegate tasks, never the accountability.
Internal assessment has two layers: ongoing monitoring inside daily work and periodic self-assessment. Results go to the board and senior management at least yearly, with action plans for gaps.

An external assessment is due at least every five years; the qualified, independent assessor or team includes at least one active CIA. The board approves the plan and gets the complete results directly.
Cannot conform? Document and communicate the circumstance, the alternative actions, their impact and the rationale. A law that blocks one part never excuses the rest.

Match the disclosure to its reach: one engagement in its final communication, the whole function to the board and senior management. Claim conformance only where supervision and the quality program support it.
The chief audit executive develops performance objectives with board and senior management input; the board approves them at least yearly. A shortfall needs an action plan.
Every indicator needs a target. Avoid measures that reward the number of findings or the audited managers' approval, and read efficiency only beside coverage and quality.
Seven required qualities: clear, concise, complete, accurate, objective, constructive and timely. Name the flaw by the fix it needs; objective means balanced, not soft.

Every final communication: objectives, scope, conclusions, recommendations or action plans, owners and dates. Assurance adds findings with significance and priority, scope limitations and a conclusion on effectiveness.
Management owns the action. A good plan reaches the root cause, has an owner and a date, and brings the risk within tolerance. Repairing the items found is only a start.

Internal auditors draft; the chief audit executive reviews and approves before issue and decides who receives it. A release outside the organization waits for legal or senior management advice as required.
A finding fixed before issue is reported with the action acknowledged, never deleted. A significant error is corrected promptly for everyone who received the original.

Accepted risk above appetite or tolerance: the responsible management first (a should), then senior management (a must), then the board if unresolved (a must). The chief audit executive never resolves it.

Follow up by inquiry, risk-based assessment and tracking, scaled to significance. A missed date: document management's explanation and take it to the chief audit executive, who judges whether the delay means risk beyond tolerance has been accepted.

principles.intro: The mindset principles, one line each. Read a few a day this week, starting with the family behind your most common slip.

priority_words.meaning: Order. Accepted risk goes to the responsible management, then senior management, then the board if unresolved. A plan is assessed, discussed, then approved. Discussion comes before escalation.
priority_words.cue: Ask: which step does this one depend on?

priority_words.meaning: Several options would help. Pick the one that keeps the chief audit executive in their seat: proposing, reporting and escalating, with approval left to the board and action to management.
priority_words.cue: Ask: which one keeps me in my seat?

priority_words.meaning: A ranking on one named quality, such as most important to report to the board or most useful performance measure. Judge the options on that quality only.
The main purpose or reason, not a side benefit. Follow-up exists to confirm that management acted; a quality program exists to show conformance and drive improvement.
priority_words.cue: Ask: why does this exist at all?

priority_words.meaning: The largest amount of the named quality. For a finding or an accepted risk, weigh likelihood and impact against the organization's appetite or tolerance, not the money alone.
priority_words.cue: Ask: greatest what, and against which limit?

priority_words.meaning: Probability, not severity. What the facts given most probably point to, such as what a pattern of missed action dates means, even if another outcome would be worse.
priority_words.cue: Ask: what usually follows from these facts?

priority_words.meaning: Rare on CIA questions, which usually ask for the right answer. If you meet it, flip the test: three options fit, and you want the one that fits least. Slow down.
priority_words.cue: Ask: which one does not belong?

answering_routine.title: Read the last line first
answering_routine.text: Find what is asked: an action, a person, a document, a report or a reason.

answering_routine.title: Function or engagement?
answering_routine.text: Is it the whole function (strategy, plan, budget, people, quality) or an engagement's results and follow-up? An option from one engagement's fieldwork is often the trap.

answering_routine.title: Find the actor and the priority word
answering_routine.text: Chief audit executive, internal auditors, the board, senior management or the management responsible? Then find the priority word, written in lowercase, such as “first”, “best”, “most”, “primary” or “most likely”, before you read the options.

answering_routine.title: Eliminate two
answering_routine.text: Strike options where the chief audit executive decides for management or the board, approval is sought where no Standard requires it, a step in the route is skipped, or a should is called a must.

answering_routine.title: Settle the final two with a principle
answering_routine.text: Ask who approves, who must be told and when, and who owns the action. Say the reason in one sentence, then answer.

pace: 100 questions in 120 minutes is 1.2 minutes each. Use that to set checkpoints, not to time each question.
Checkpoints: question 50 by minute 60; question 75 by minute 90. Look at the clock there and otherwise leave it alone.
Ahead at a checkpoint? Those minutes are your review time. Behind? Decide a little faster on the next few; do not rush them all.
Stuck? Choose your best answer and move on. Wrong answers are not penalized, so never leave a blank.
No breaks are scheduled, and the clock keeps running if you take one.
Change an answer when you find a clear reason, such as an actor, a must or should, or a priority word you missed the first time.
